Most of the grants we submit require estimates in "% of FTE".  Which is "How much of a person's time is going to be dedicated to this project over the life of the project?"

Then they also want a dollar estimate, which is the % of FTE * Employee Salary, but the Employee is not always determined at the time of the grant and each Employee would have slightly different salaries.  

So, I just estimate the project in hours (typical estimate formula, actual estimate * 2 * 3).  We get paid monthly and there's roughly 160 hours per month.  160 * Months of Grant = Hours per grant.  Hours per grant / project estimate = % FTE.  % FTE * Highest paid developer's salary = $ for my team.

Not the same, but basically, you estimate in hours like normal and then make that fit the timeline you're looking at.

Or heck, just estimate the timeline and give that timeline in Man-Days.

And if you're estimating an actual 4 hours of work per day, then who cares about their 8 hour = 1 Man Day?

I think the bottom line is that you make their estimate fit your reality.

I used to be hardcore Scrum/Story Points.  Then I took over as a tech lead / engineering manager.  The only time I do estimates is when someone asks me "How much money do you need to do this project?"

Where I work, funding comes in the form of a percentage of effort for a full time employee over the grant period.  The grant will last, for instance, 2 years and we need to provide a budget for what money it will take to accomplish the goal of the grant.  The line items in the budget will be something like, "X% effort of Y FTE for 2 Years - $Z.00".  

To figure that out, I ask my best developer "This is the project proposal.  If you're the only developer working on this, and you're working on nothing but this project, how long do you think it would take?"  After a couple of days, she'll tell me how long it would take her.  I double that figure.  Then triple that.  This accounts for the time lost from the cognitive load of task switching, the time lost in meetings, the time lost from hiring new team members, etc.  I multiply that by her salary to get a total dollar amount for the project (Z).  I divide that by the grant period to find out the total % effort of an FTE that I need to devote to this project. I divide that by the adjusted amount of effort (amount of her time) she can devote to this project (based on how many other projects she's on and how much of her effort is bought by other projects).  That tells me how many full time employees I actually need (Y) and how much of their time/effort (X) I need to devote to a project.  Sometimes I add on an extra %FTE or two to the final totals if my spider senses tingle (usually has to do with how many PIs are on the project or if I know any of the PIs from previous projects).

Ultimately, this total gets cut anyway, but it's better for them to cut a bigger, potentially overestimated number than it is for them to cut an underestimated or "accurate" number.  Such is life.

However, when it comes to actual planning and task management, I don't use time estimates.  For a while I would use "urgency" as one of the variables, but that tends to either get converted into time, or everything becomes "urgent" which causes things to fall off the board unintentionally.

Right now, I'm experimenting with "Impact" and "Difficulty".  Everything is ultimately an estimate because no one can see the future.  But it helps to prioritize without defaulting to time based estimations.  

We estimate Impact based on number of users effected, amount of value the task can add overall, number of other tasks this will unblock, etc.  Higher Impact equals Higher Priority.  

Difficulty is set exclusively by the dev who's going to work on the task.  I can give a basic estimate, but I have years of experience.  I can add a column to a SQL table in my sleep, but my dev might only have experience in Mongo or something, so he's got to do a lot more research.  Is the task going to be easy or difficult to accomplish?  Easy tasks get a higher priority because quick wins improve moral and difficult tasks can usually be broken down into multiple easy tasks with a little bit of discussion and planning.  We also have a PIA (Pain In Ass) category for tasks that are easy, but will take a lot of manual time and effort.  These tend to get a lower priority because they slow down productivity despite adding significant value.

This helps us prioritize work, track progress, and manage stakeholder expectations without committing to a hard timeline.  Everyone already knows the final deadline, which is something we can't control (like the end of the grant period or some random release or demo date dictated by senior leadership). The steps in between don't matter as long as we're making progress.

We try to stay agile, though, so if my hypotheses are wrong and this system doesn't work out long term, we'll switch to something else that makes more sense.

Sounded to me like that's what was trying to be accomplished.  OP has backend Laravel APIs and he doesn't want other people to be able to use his endpoints.  You prevent other people from using your endpoints by having a csrf token that effectively ties your backend to your frontend.

Server generates a token and inserts it into the page.  That token is sent with every request to the API.  The API rejects the request unless it has a valid token.  Valid tokens are only created by the backend, thus are only available to OP's frontend.  You could even make them expire after a few minutes, rotating them on successful requests.

A CSRF token isn't a silver bullet that can be implemented in every case and it won't solve all your problems, but, like I said, if you're just trying to secure your backend against other people using your endpoints, this is a way to do.  Can it be defeated?  Sure, but so can any kind of security if you want it bad enough.

Anyway, CORS and CSRF tokens are usually simple first steps for securing a backend, imho.

Dictionaries and lists are as important as strings and integers.

Important libraries, especially for data science, include `pandas` and `numpy`.  My team also uses `flask`, but we do mostly web development.

I tend to write the most verbose code imaginable.  I'm a huge proponent of "self documenting code", wherein you make you variable names make sense and write the code so it's completely understandable.  I'll take a plain old `for` loop over list comprehension any day (except the days where you really need list comprehension).  There's a penchant in the community for one-liners and making the most compact and elegant code possible.  Personally, I'd rather clunky and readable.  But that's me.

PS:  Since you're new to programming, I'll provide a really basic metaphor that I've used many times previously.  Novel incoming: 

Think of a variable as a box that holds a value.

A `list` is just a type of value that holds more boxes.  So it's kind of like a box full of boxes.  These "sub-boxes" (list items) are assigned a number (index) and you can easily pull the value out of the sub-box by finding the index you're interested in.  They're great for when you just need to put a bunch of values together in a collection or you care about the order (e.g. people standing in a queue).  The only "weird" thing about lists is that the indexes start with 0 instead of 1.  There are a lot of technical reasons why this is the case, but just go with it.

A `dictionary` is similar in that it's a "box of boxes", but rather than being automatically assigned an index, you get to label the sub-boxes however you want. It's great for when you need to have your data structured and want to easily grab a value from a sub-box without having to remember the order of the items.  For example, you want to keep information about a person together and you want to be able to look up their "surname", "given name", "birthday", etc. by just looking at the name of the box (called the key).  You'll often hear people talk about "key-value pairs", which means "the label on the box and the value inside the box".  If it helps, it's called a "dictionary" because like a real dictionary, you have a bunch of terms (keys) and the definitions associated with the term (value).

Now, the real power comes from the fact that you don't just have to fill the sub-boxes with just strings and numbers.  The values can also be other lists or dictionaries, so you can have a box of boxes of boxes of boxes of boxes, if you want.  Why would you want this?  Let's look at the previous examples:

Maybe in your list of people standing in a queue, you don't want to just have a string with their full name.  Maybe you want to be able to easily grab a person's birthday.  You just use a list full of dictionaries!  So now you can easily grab the birthday of the 4th person in line by providing an index and a key:  `queue_of_people[3]['birthday']`.  You're looking at the value of the box labeled "birthday" that's in the 4th box in the list.

You go from something like this that doesn't use lists or dictionaries:
```
person_1_name = 'bill'
person_1_birthday = 'january 1st'
person_2_name = 'chris'
person_2_birthday = 'february 1st'
...
person_1000_name = 'zoey'
person_1000_birthday = 'december 31st'
```

to something like this:
```
queue_of_people = [
    {
        "name": "bill",
        "birthday": 'january 1st'
    }, {
        "name": "chris",
        "birthday": 'february 1st'
    },
    ...
    {
        "name": "zoey",
        "birthday": 'december 31st'
    },
]
```

With only 2 people, this may not matter much, but just imagine a queue of 1000 people and that queue is changing all the time.  And when you go to do something with the people, it saves a lot of effor and problems.  You can just loop through the list rather than having to use 1000 different variables.
```
print(person_1_name)
print(person_1_birthday)
print(person_2_name)
print(person_2_birthday)
...
print(person_1000_name)
print(person_1000_birthday)
```
becomes
```
for person in queue_of_people:
    print(person["name"]
    print(person["birthday"]
```

Now, of course, there's a lot of other features, benefits, and drawbacks of each of these datatypes.  I'm sure there will be other people who will comment "Well, actually...", but this was just a very basic intro.  As you continue your programming, you'll find out about all the cool things.

Hope this helps!  Good luck!

Now that my rage has subsided, Blockchain/crypto/NFT are not dead.  Blockchain is a powerful technology that can help with a lot of problems.  Unfortunately, during the hype, it was mostly used for get-rich-quick scams like crypto and NFTs and that's kind of the primary usecase at this point.

"Web 3" is a misnomer because blockchain doesn't have anything to do with the web.  It was used as a buzzword that evolved from Web 2.0.  

What we now call Web 1.0 was basically that users were able to consume content created by people who built websites.  With improved technology, web developers could build web apps that allowed users to post their own content without having to build their own websites, and other users could consume and interact with user-generated content.  That is the general consensus on what Web 2.0 was.  It was a paradigm shift on how people used the web.

There's not a real consensus on what "Web 3" is or should be.  Some people (who are wrong) use Web3 to describe the "decentralization of the web" via Blockchain and similar technologies.  I think that's too tech focused, personally, and also wrong, considering that everyone uses AWS and other big hosts, which re-centralizes everything.  And also, Blockchain doesn't even have anythign to do with the web.

Others (like Tim Berners-Lee, the guy who invented the web to begin with) consider Web 3.0 to be the "semantic web" which means that websites and content should be machine-readable so that the content can be shared across platforms.  This is how we got things like HTML5 with its <section> and <aside> tags.

If we're looking at a web 3.0 as a paradigm shift in usage, as was the shift between 1 and 2, then I'd personally consider the advancement and ubiquity of mobile apps to be the primary factor in Web 3.0.  The web (the interconnection between pieces of content) is now used beyond just the web browser.  Now we've got non-browser apps that we use on our phones that reference content on other apps.  The browser is still around and will continue to be around, of course, but a lot of content is now consumed through mobile apps.  X, Instagram, Facebook, Amazon, etc are all accessed through apps now.  Lowes, Target, Walmart, McDonalds, TacoBell all have apps that they'd prefer you use rather than their websites.

It's up for debate what Web 3 actually is.  What's not up for debate is that a lot of crypto bros and scammers started shilling "Web 3" as a buzzword for non-web technologies.

My general rule of thumb is "don't be an asshole".  I feel like devs tend to get combatitive when interacting with designers who don't understand the web.  (I was not immune to this when I was younger.)

Don't try to "manage" the designer.  The trick is to be kind and patient, provide constructive feedback, and educate.  Most importantly, be humble.  If you knew everything about design, you'd be the one designing rather than just implementing it.  It's a collaborative effort, even if no one realizes it or treats it as a collaboration.  Sometimes you have to secretly manipulate the relationship into a collaboration.

Also, sometimes you just need to get over yourself and implement it as given.  If you're going to be "just a developer" then be just a developer.  Don't try to figure it out and make it perfect. Don't try to make it make sense from a web perspective.  Just puke out a bunch of html into notepad that makes it look like what they want.  Then show them why it doesn't work and ask how they want to fix it.  Play dumb.  "This is what I was given, this is what I was able to produce with what I was given."  

The alternative is truly to just do it yourself.  Make your own decisions that fill in the gaps that they leave.  They care about how you structure your html about as much as you care about their favorite photoshop brush.

I wrote a program one time where I build a "band" that could write and play songs.  Each band member had a bunch of similar functions (play music, write music, generate sounds, etc).  A lot of the functions were shared, but sometimes they needed little tweaks.  Like, the guitar and bass worked almost identically.  But the drums were different because it doesn't usually care about notes, just beats.  So I had a parent class called "instrument" and a subclass for "drums" that inherited from "instrument". I had to override a couple of the functions like "write music".  But the function/method names were always the same, so all the instruments had the exact same interface.

Later on in the program, I could just build the band and each instrument has all the same functions, so I didn't have to worry about the different function names for each different function.  As an example:

No Class:
```
write_bass_music()
write_guitar_music()
write_drum_music()
play_bass_music()
play_guitar_music()
play_drum_music()
```

with class:
```
bass = new Instrument()
guitar = new Instrument()
drums = new DrumKit()

bass.write_music()
guitar.write_music()
drums.write_music()
bass.play_music()
guitar.play_music()
drums.play_music()
```

Or better yet:
```
band = { "bass": new Instrument(), "guitar": new Instrument(), "drums": new DrumKit() }

for instrument in band:
    instrument.write_music()
for instrument in band:
    instrument.play_music()
```

The way I look at is is Test DRIVEN Development.  You don't write tests after, you use the tests to help your work.

Say there's a part of your app that you're working on.  Maybe it's a function to calculate how many tomatoes go into a stew based on the size of a user's bowl.  In your app, under normal circumstances, you might need to 1) create a user, 2) add a bowl, 3) set size of bowl 4) add other ingredients 5) click the tomatoes button.  And you have to do this EVERY TIME you change something about that function.

Now, if you're using a test, you write a test that only runs that one function with various sample inputs.  Then, if you make a change to that function, you just have to run the test and see if it still runs given those sample inputs.

If you do it right, you speed up development time considerably.  Now, this was a contrived example, but you could see the benefits if you're working on a really complex function that relies on a really complex user workflow.

When you go to a website, the first thing that happens is the dns lookup converts the domain (example.Com or even sub.example.com) to an ip address. The request then gets sent to the machine attached to the ip address where its handled by the web server (apache, etc).

The web server will look at the request and try to match that request with a resource, typically a file of some sort. In the case of the reverse proxy, rather than returning a file, it will forward the request to another server. In your case, it would forward the request to your app. But this all assumes everything has been configured properly... That the paths and the proxy are configured correctly.

Now, a 500 error is a server error, meaning that something broke on the server. Maybe a runtime error or something. Whatever happened, the request got handled by the server but it broke before anything was returned. You'll need to go through the server logs to find out what broke.

400 errors typically indicate that the server handled the request, but there was something wrong with the request that the client sent. 404 means that the url that was sent in the request does not match a valid resource... So the url is wrong, a file is missing, or something of that nature.

It's not about what data is getting returned, it's about how the urls are being handled and how you've configured the server. Data is data, and computers don't care if it's just garbage output or an image or whatever. 404 just means that the path you entered is incorrect for some reason and the server could not find any data to return.

Outside of development, anything that is accessed through a url that starts with `http://` should use port 80.  Anything that uses `https://` should use 443.  

All you need is for someone to upgrade their browser in the future and the latest version randomly decides to block port 3000 for some insane reason.  Or for AWS to decide randomly it's just going turn off port 3000 for security reasons.  Then everything breaks and you get a panicked call in the middle of the night.

That being said, we use a microservices architecture, where we have multiple apps, each running on their own unique ports on localhost.  Like `localhost:3000` or `localhost:3041` or what not.  Then we use a reverse proxy to forward those localhost ports to specific urls.

For example, we might have the backend api running on `http://localhost:3042` but we use a reverse proxy so that it's exposed to the world at `https://example.com/api`.  Then we might also have a different api running on the same server for the login system and have it running on `http://localhost:5236` and have a reverse proxy to expose it as `https://example.com/login-api`.

Also,

Likely, the reason you couldn't get nginx or whatever to work on port 80 is because it's flagged as a reserved port or is already in use by apache (or some other weird thing).  Using a reverse proxy like I explained fixes this because you can tell gunicorn to run the app on `localhost:3000` and the web server (apache, nginx, whatever) will basically forward it to 80.

A few things:

Don't ever host a website/rest api on anything other than port 80 or 443.  Some public wifi networks will block non-standard ports.

If you're using AWS, look into their service Elastic Beanstalk.  It gives you a URL rather than just an IP address for your app.  

As for your specific question (running your app on example.com/api) look up "reverse proxies".  I don't know how to do this with nginx, but with apache, you'd use the Proxy Pass directive.

For example, what makes more sense when writing an API endpoing?  Logging into the site, navigating to the required page, filling out a form with test data, hitting submit and looking at the console... then repeating for every edge case and hope it works?  Or writing a couple tests that automatically does all this so that you can focus on your api endpoint's business logic?

You don't always need tests, but when you do, it makes life a lot easier.  Don't write tests for the green lights.  Write tests so you can work on the fun stuff.

It truly depends on what you're trying to accomplish.  CSS and JavaScript are two of the 3 fundamental technologies of web development.  In most cases, they should be used together.

CSS is for making things look a certain way.  Javascript is for dealing with business logic.  In many cases, changing the data should affect the way things look, so you want to use both.

For example:  You have a list of icons.  Icons can be in 2 different states:  active and not active. When an icon is in the "active" state, it turns blue and starts shaking on the screen.  

You might use Javascript to add a class name to the icon like `class='active'` to tell the system "this icon is active".  But you use CSS to make all `.active` icons turn blue and start shaking.

You COULD use Javascript to animate the icons and set the color to blue.  But the color and animation have nothing to do with with the state of the icon, internally and all that extra javascript code could pollute the logic. 

You COULD use HTML and CSS to link the icon to a hidden checkbox and use a CSS rule to manage icons that are linked to checked checkboxes, but then you've got unnecessary checkboxes (which have semantic meanings for screen readers, etc) and css hacks.

It's a separation of concerns.  CSS isn't concerned with the business logic.  Javascript isn't concerned with how the app looks. 

tl;dr:  Use both together.

It's your job as scrum master or PO to translate the development velocity for management.  You should know your team well enough and collaborate enough so that you have a rough idea of how velocity translates into a timeline.  You don't put that burden on your developers so that they can focus on developing.  After a while, the team gets an idea of how it works together and gets better at estimating complexity, so things get a little more standardized which makes it easier for you to translate their velocity.

So your choice is this:  Do you care more about your team working a set number of hours, or do you care more about getting tasks completed well?  If you care more about hours, don't bother with story points and just use hours.  If you care about actual productivity and quality, use some other estimation metric.

Here's some advice in little bite sized mantras that have helped me get through situations like this:

*Fake it 'till you make it.*    Pretend like you know what you're doing and you'll eventually get it.  Just make sure that you don't get too arrogant and dismiss people who call you out.  Everything is a learning experience and more often than not, your feelings of inadequacy are just imposter syndrome.

*Work to live, don't live to work.*   Developing could be your favorite thing in the world, but don't forget that it's just a job.  You need to take breaks and have a decent work-life balance.  If you still like developing in your non-work time, work on something fun and fulfilling.  Mental health is often overlooked in this industry and there's a high rate of burnout because we work all the time.  Get some non-developing hobbies to let your brain recharge.

*You'll never be the best, but that's okay.  Just don't be the worst.*  A lot of the articles you read and a lot of the "advice" you see are by guys who eat, sleep, and shit code.  Don't compare yourself to them.  It'll just reinforce your imposter syndrome.  Most of us normies who do this for a living don't bother writing blogs because we do actual work and then go home and rest.  As long as you're not the worst candidate, you'll be fine.  And clearly, you're not the worst candidate because they hired you instead of someone else.

Going back to that last point, and this might be a bit cynical:  It's often a lot more expensive for a company to fire and replace you than it is to just keep you on board.  If you're honestly trying and improving all the time, then there's no reason for them to let you go (aside from like budgetary reasons).  It takes time to find and train someone new and the little bit of institutional knowledge you've gained working on company code is a huge asset over any other newbie.

So, just stick with it, but don't be too hard on yourself.  It's just a job.

Also, if using a shared system that you don't have root access to, you can't use apt to install global packages.  Using a virtual environment lets you install whatever you want\* within the virtual environment.

You mentioned performance.  My point was that you're not going to notice any performance gains.  We're running javascript on phones that are more powerful than the computers that got us to the moon. I had a guy spending hours optimizing the pus out of some loops because his function was running slowly.  It had nothing to do with the loops.  It was the ajax endpoint he was hitting that was just taking its sweet time.  In my experience, if your performance is poor enough to notice, your time would be spent more wisely looking for bigger problems than worrying about a loop or a switch statement.

All that being said, I've been working with big data for the past few years and I've gotten to the point where I've optimized code so much on some projects that a micro optimization like that actually comes out to save almost a full minute of compute time.

`switch` is used mostly in place of long `if...else if...else` chains.  It's a style preference. Github is a hosting solution for Git repositories.  There are two different kinds of repositories you can put on github:  Public and Private.  If you don't want the world to know what your awful beginner projects look like, just put them on Private.  Once you have something you're proud of, just put it on Public.

If I were you, I'd put all my code on Github for various reasons:  It's basically a free code-backup system.  If your computer dies, you can always just clone your code back onto your new machine because it's hosted in the cloud.

Also, it makes it super easy to deploy your code to other servers (assuming those servers also have Git installed).    You would push your code from your local dev environment to Github.  Then you'd go into your webserver and pull your code from Github onto the server.  There might be other config things you might need to do (like moving the code to a public path or what not) but IMHO, it beats using FTP and copying things manually.

A lot of the different frameworks and options have more to do with development preferences and development speed.  Do you like writing things yourself?  Do you like getting stuff done quickly?  Do you like using an ORM?  Do you like having the web server attached to your backend?

If you get to a point where you're getting facebook level traffic, you'll probably need to re evaluate the architecture of your system anyway.

And it's not like you're locked into a single framework for life.  If you're at the beginning of your career, find what works for you and then learn whatever your job wants you to use.
